clues.title: Plate: long yellow with blue strip
text: The Netherlands has long, **yellow licence plates** with the standard European blue strip on the left. Dutch taxis have blue plates.

NOTE: The only other countries in Europe with yellow licence plates are Luxembourg and the UK. For the UK, only the back plates are yellow, and they often lack the blue strip. In addition, some older coverage in France features the French yellow back plates. In Denmark, you can find yellow plates on commercial vehicles.
clues.summary: Long yellow plates with the blue European strip on the left. Taxis have blue plates. Yellow plates also exist in Luxembourg and the UK (rear only), and on Danish commercial vehicles.

differs.how: only rear plates are yellow, often no blue strip

clues.title: Language: double vowels, ij, ieuw, oe
text: **Dutch** is a Germanic language. It features a lot of double vowels. Typical letter clusters are ij, ieuw and oe. “IJ“ written as one capitalised letter is also unique to the language.
NOTE: Dutch is also used in the region of Flanders, which comprises the northern half of Belgium.

images.caption: Dutch text with IJ shown large

clues.summary: A Germanic language with lots of double vowels and clusters like ij, ieuw and oe. A single capital IJ is unique to it. Also spoken in northern Belgium.

clues.title: Bollard: plain white, red reflector
text: The Netherlands has a simple, white **bollard** with a red reflector.

NOTE: On rare occasions, you can find round [French-style bollards](https://goo.gl/maps/vTgbpvfX35mcng4k8) with a red band and a pointed top. A difference with French bollards is that the red wrap usually does not go all the way around the bollard.
clues.summary: A simple white bollard with a red reflector. Rarely, round French-style bollards appear, but their red band usually doesn't wrap fully around.

differs.how: French red band goes all the way around

clues.title: Pole: no street-level utility poles
text: The Netherlands usually **does not have any utility poles**. You might see larger power lines like the ones shown in the image, but essentially never any street-level smaller utility poles.
NOTE: Belgium does use utility poles somewhat commonly.
clues.summary: Almost no small utility poles, only big power lines. Belgium uses utility poles fairly often.

clues.title: Landscape: extremely flat, below sea level
text: The Netherlands is extraordinarily **flat**. In most of the country, you will get no more than a few metres of elevation. Large swathes of the country are reclaimed land that is at or even below sea level.
NOTE: The most major exception to this is the south of Limburg, where you can get low hills. Another place with some amount of hills is De Veluwe in central Gelderland province.
clues.summary: Extremely flat, with only a few metres of height difference in most places. Large areas are reclaimed land at or below sea level. Low hills exist in the far south and in a central forest area.

clues.title: Landscape: waterways, canals, dikes
text: In addition, the Netherlands is a very water-rich country. The country has innumerous **waterways**. Canals and ditches next to the road are common. Water management is an important facet of Dutch infrastructure, so you will often see [dikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levee) (low earthen walls to protect against water), dams and bridges.
clues.summary: Countless waterways. Canals and ditches beside the road are common, along with dikes (low earth walls), dams and bridges.

clues.title: Roads: rows of trees along rural roads
text: Many rural roads are **lined by rows of trees**.
NOTE: This is also common in Poland.
clues.summary: Many country roads are lined with rows of trees. Common in Poland too.

clues.title: Towns: very organised, planned suburbs
text: The Netherlands has a high amount of urban planning, and as a result tends to have a **very organised look**. Road infrastructure is well-maintained. Suburbs are usually master-planned and typically feature row houses.
clues.summary: A tidy, planned look with well-kept roads. Suburbs are master-planned and usually made of row houses.

clues.title: Road lines: all white, dashed edge lines
text: Like most of Europe, the Netherlands has **all-white** road lines. Many roads have dashed outside lines. Sometimes, you can find unique [green middle lines](https://goo.gl/maps/hFMtuu8BBeGNQbiPA).
clues.summary: All white lines, as in most of Europe, and many roads have dashed edge lines. Occasionally green centre lines appear.

clues.title: Roadside: bike paths, often reddish-pink
text: Many Dutch roads are flanked by **bicycle paths**. Different designs exist, but a very common one is a reddish-pink lane.
Cycling is one of the most common modes of transportation in the Netherlands. You will see cyclists and bicycles everywhere.
clues.summary: Many roads have bicycle paths beside them, often a reddish-pink lane. Cyclists are everywhere.

clues.title: Road: brick paving
text: **Brick roads** are common in the Netherlands, both in rural and urban areas. The brick pattern shown in the image is especially common.

images.caption: Red circle marks herringbone brick paving along the road

clues.summary: Brick roads are common in towns and countryside, often in one particular pattern.

clues.title: Sidewalk: square grey tiles, offset pattern
text: Most Dutch **sidewalks** use the same type of square grey tiles and offset tiling pattern. In some historic areas, you might find smaller [brick sidewalks](https://goo.gl/maps/57mi9meFyFNVCbun9).

images.caption: Sidewalk tiles compared: common grey tiles (left) and historic red brick (right)

clues.summary: Most sidewalks use square grey tiles laid in an offset pattern. Some old areas have small brick sidewalks.

clues.title: Speed bump: long and short white stripes
text: The Netherlands has very recognizable **speed bumps**. They usually have white warning stripes that alternate between long and short. The example image is on a brick road, but they also occur on [asphalt roads](https://goo.gl/maps/QsuN5WtHsjZ2EoeJ9).
clues.summary: Speed bumps with white warning stripes alternating long and short, on brick and on asphalt.

clues.title: Roadside: brick rumble strip
text: Many rural roads feature a sort of **brick rumble strip** on the sides. This is fairly unique to the Netherlands and a good way to identify the country in very rural rounds.

images.caption: Circle zooms in on the brick rumble strip beside the cycle path

clues.summary: Many country roads have a strip of bricks along the edge, almost unique and useful on very rural roads.

clues.title: Street sign: blue with white text, straat
text: Street signs are almost always **blue with white lettering**. Very rarely, you can find [yellow](https://goo.gl/maps/yMhbRKLJK1QuyEs68), [white](https://goo.gl/maps/8TuTmC7n7oLw8qAS9) or [green](https://goo.gl/maps/W3BrcUwTrYA4TeMC8) street signs.

The Dutch word for street is **straat**. Other common road name endings are -weg, -laan, -pad, and -plein. However, if you see a blue sign with the word ‘fietspad’, do not search for it; it simply means ‘bicycle path’.
NOTE: Street signs in Belgium come in a variety of colours and usually mention the municipality, which is rare in the Netherlands.
clues.summary: Street signs are almost always blue with white text. Rarely yellow, white or green. Names end in straat, -weg, -laan, -pad, -plein. 'Fietspad' just means bike path. Belgium's signs vary in colour and name the municipality.

differs.how: signs vary in colour and show the municipality

clues.title: Sign: blue direction signs, white bike signs
text: Dutch **direction signs** are blue with white lettering. Signs for bicyclists are [white with a red border](https://goo.gl/maps/Ym8jxRtVRgdeJFgf6).
clues.summary: Direction signs are blue with white text. Signs for cyclists are white with a red border.

clues.title: Sign: blue town entry with municipality
text: Dutch **town entry signs** are blue. The signs sometimes have very [elaborate designs](https://goo.gl/maps/XAfoVPzYZfX83KoS9), often with frames and additional signs.

NOTE: Often, these signs list the municipality they are in, after the word ‘gemeente’ (gem). Many municipalities are named after larger towns or cities in the vicinity, which can help a lot with scanning.
clues.summary: Blue town entry signs, sometimes elaborate with frames and extra signs. They often show the municipality after 'gemeente' (gem), which is often named after a nearby bigger town.

clues.title: Route marker: green with A or N number
text: Dutch **road markers** are green. Many list the road number in a small yellow or red box.
Highways have a red box and start with the letter **A**. Regional roads have a yellow box and start with the letter **N**.
NOTE: Some of them have province-specific designs. You can learn more about this in the region-guessing section.
clues.summary: Green road markers with the number in a small box. Motorways have a red box and start with A, regional roads a yellow box and N. Some have province-specific designs.

clues.title: Sign: edge border visible from behind
text: Edges of Dutch road signs will extend to the back, creating a **border visible from behind**, sometimes retaining the colour of the sign. This is both consistent and unique to the country.
clues.summary: Road sign edges wrap around to the back, giving a border visible from behind, sometimes in the sign's colour. Consistent and unique.

clues.title: Sign: striped signposts, black-white or blue-white
text: Many Dutch signposts feature **striped markings** with a black-and-white or blue-and-white colour scheme.
clues.summary: Many signposts have stripes in black and white or blue and white.

clues.title: Sign: bulky yellow signpost on islands
text: Road signs on traffic islands often have these bulky **yellow signposts**.
clues.summary: Road signs on traffic islands often sit on bulky yellow posts.

clues.title: Guardrail: striped barrier
text: On some roads, especially in rural areas, you might find these distinctive **striped barriers**.
clues.summary: Distinctive striped barriers on some roads, especially in the countryside.

clues.title: Houses: red-brown brick, orange or grey tiles
text: **Brick architecture** is very common in the Netherlands. Many buildings feature red-brownish-coloured bricks. Roofs often have orange or dark grey tiles.
NOTE: Similar brick architecture is also common in Denmark and Belgium.
clues.summary: Brick buildings are very common, mostly red-brown, with orange or dark grey roof tiles. Denmark and Belgium look similar.

clues.title: Houses: row houses everywhere
text: As mentioned before, **row houses** are very common in the Netherlands. Almost half of the Dutch housing stock are row houses, significantly more than almost all other European countries.
clues.summary: Almost half of all homes are row houses, far more than in most European countries.

clues.title: Landmark: windmills and wind turbines
text: **Windmills**, both traditional water or grain mills, and modern [wind power turbines](https://goo.gl/maps/opan2kvhD6DRGkRU9), are common in the Netherlands.
clues.summary: Both traditional water or grain windmills and modern wind turbines are common.

clues.title: Google car: black back showing through blur
text: Some Generation 4 coverage has a car blur glitch where the **black back of the Google car** is visible.
clues.summary: In some Gen 4 coverage a glitch in the blur shows the black back of the Google car.

clues.title: Google car: low-mounted camera, big round blur
text: The Netherlands also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of Western Europe also has smallcam.

images.caption: Four panels labelled front panned down, front panned straight, back panned down and good blur (front)

clues.summary: A Gen 4 camera mounted lower than normal, with a fairly large round blur and a small bump at the front. The blur can be see-through. Most of Western Europe has it.

clues.title: Phone numbers: 3-4 digit area codes, mobile 06
text: Dutch landline phone numbers start with a three- or four-digit **area code**. These are geographically grouped, except for the ones that start with 07, and two of the 02 codes.
NOTE: Dutch mobile phone numbers start with 06, which is a code that is not used for any of the landline area codes.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._
clues.summary: Landlines start with a 3 or 4 digit area code, grouped by region (except 07 and two 02 codes). Mobiles start with 06, which no landline code uses.

clues.title: Route marker: regional designs and km stickers
text: Some road markers (“**hectometre markers**”) have province-specific designs. This only applies to markers for regional N-roads, which have road numbers in yellow boxes.
Not all N-road markers have province-specific designs: some just have a generic design that can be found nationwide.
The A-roads all have the same signs and are recognizable because the road number is in a red box.
Bollards sometimes feature **kilometre stickers**, which are also limited to specific regions.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it. Image provided by Timzkii._
clues.summary: Regional N-road markers (yellow box) sometimes have province-specific designs, others are generic. Motorway markers (red box) are all the same. Bollards may carry region-specific km stickers.

clues.title: Flags: provincial flags, two common ones
text: All Dutch provinces have their own flag. However, most of these are very rarely seen in the wild. The major exceptions to this are the flags of **Friesland** and **Noord-Brabant**.
In addition, you can sometimes see the unofficial but very popular flag of the Achterhoek cultural region in the east of Gelderland.
For a full list of all provincial flags, you can view [this Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flags_of_provinces_of_the_Netherlands).
clues.summary: Every province has its own flag, but most are rarely seen. The Friesland and Noord-Brabant flags are common, and an unofficial flag of the Achterhoek region in the east is popular.

clues.title: Language: ^ vowels, wei or strjitte endings
text: In the province of Friesland, the Frisian language is commonly spoken. While Dutch language is still most prevalent on signs, a lot of town entry signs will feature **bilingual town names**.
Some street names in Friesland uniquely end in -wei or -strjitte.

NOTE: Frisian has vowels with [circumflex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumflex) diacritics (“little hats”): Â, Ê, Ô and Û. Dutch does not have these letters, except in loanwords. In addition, the Y is significantly more common compared to Dutch.
clues.summary: In the northern province, Frisian is spoken, so many town signs show two names. Some streets end in -wei or -strjitte. Frisian has letters Â, Ê, Ô, Û and uses Y a lot more than Dutch.

clues.title: Lamp post: tall white sticker, 3-4 digits
text: This long, vertically arranged white sticker with three to four digits is found on street lights in Limburg.
clues.summary: A long vertical white sticker with three or four digits on street lights is found in the far south-east.

clues.title: Lamp post: horizontal white sticker, 1-2 digits
text: Similarly to Limburg, North Brabant also has white stickers on their street lights, however it is horizontally arranged and only has one or two digits.

images.caption: Circle shows the horizontal white lamp post sticker with two digits

clues.summary: The southern province next to it also has white stickers on street lights, but horizontal with only one or two digits.

clues.title: Landscape: marshy polder, many small waterways
text: Most of the **west and north** is at or below sea-level. As a result, most of this region’s countryside has a distinct [“**polder**” landscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polder): the landscape is marshy, often with a large amount of small waterways.
clues.summary: The west and north are at or below sea level, with marshy 'polder' countryside full of small waterways.

clues.title: Landscape: typical flat farmland
text: Conversely, the **south and the east** tends to have a more typical flat European farmland look. Waterways are still common, but the landscape can look less marshy.
clues.summary: The south and east look like ordinary flat European farmland. Waterways exist but the land is less marshy.

clues.title: Landscape: low hills in the far south
text: While most of the Netherlands is very flat, Southern Limburg has some **low hills**.
clues.summary: Southern Limburg has some low hills, unlike the rest of the very flat country.

clues.title: Landscape: forest, heath and sandy soil
text: The **Veluwe** area is unusually forested for Dutch standards. Some parts feature a very slight amount of elevation.

Some parts of the Veluwe feature old-growth forest, [heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heath) or sandy soil. This area can [look odd](https://goo.gl/maps/6pZWyZjMDKwaZoGh6) and unlike the rest of the Netherlands if you have never seen it before.
NOTE: Some other natural areas in the Netherlands can have a similar look, but the Veluwe is by far the largest.
clues.summary: An unusually forested central area with slight elevation, old forest, heath or sandy soil. It can look odd compared with the rest of the country. Other natural areas can look similar, but this is the biggest.

clues.title: Landscape: man-made, ruler-straight roads, big fields
text: Almost all of the land belonging to the province of Flevoland was reclaimed from the sea in the mid-20th century. As a result, the province has a distinct, **man-made** look: extremely straight roads and large crop fields dominate the landscape. Wind turbines are common. In urban areas, there are no historical buildings.

NOTE: The only exception to this description is the town of Urk, which is situated on a former island now surrounded by the rest of the province’s man-made [polder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polder) landscape.
clues.summary: A province reclaimed from the sea in the mid 20th century: extremely straight roads, big crop fields, wind turbines and no historic buildings. The one exception is Urk, on a former island.

clues.title: Coast: lined with dunes
text: Most of the Dutch North Sea coast is lined by **dunes**.
clues.summary: Most of the North Sea coast is lined by sand dunes.

clues.title: Coverage: northwest islands with dunes
text: The islands in the northwest are called the **Wadden Islands**. They are very popular local tourism destinations, which is sometimes evident in the street view coverage. Their northwestern coastlines feature a lot of sand dunes.
clues.summary: The Wadden Islands in the northwest are popular tourist spots, which sometimes shows in the coverage. Their northwest coasts have lots of dunes.

clues.title: Houses: farms with very large roofs
text: Farms in the north of the Netherlands often have **very large roofs**.
clues.summary: Farms in the north often have very large roofs.

clues.title: Houses: rolling shutters in the south
text: **Rolling shutters** on house windows are more common in the southern half of the Netherlands.
NOTE: While more prevalent in the south, rolling shutters on homes in more northern regions are not unheard of. Use this meta with some caution.
clues.summary: Roll-down window shutters are more common in the southern half, but exist in the north too, so use with caution.

clues.title: Location: Caribbean island north of Venezuela
text: **Curaçao** is a constituent country in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, located north of western Venezuela in the Caribbean Sea. As such, for country streaks purposes, it is counted as the Netherlands.
Plonk It has a more in-depth guide to Curaçao [here](https://www.plonkit.net/curacao).
clues.summary: A Caribbean country in the Kingdom, north of western Venezuela. It counts as the Netherlands for streaks.

differs.how: Caribbean island with its own guide

clues.title: Street sign: district in small text below name
text: **Amsterdam street signs** feature the city district in a smaller font size below the actual street name.
NOTE: This design is very uncommon in the rest of the Netherlands.
clues.summary: The capital's street signs show the city district in smaller letters under the street name. Very uncommon elsewhere.

clues.title: Street sign: yellow text on red
text: The municipality of Oegstgeest, just northwest of Leiden, uses uniquely illegible street signs with** yellow text on a red background.**
clues.summary: One municipality near Leiden uses hard-to-read street signs with yellow text on a red background.

clues.title: Houses: green or black wood with white trim
text: Buildings in the **Zaanstreek** region just north of Amsterdam often feature wooden architectural elements, usually painted green or black; with white trims. They sometimes have [tall roof spires](https://goo.gl/maps/aLs9DTJZ3e1HMasd8), usually painted white.
clues.summary: North of the capital, buildings often have wooden parts painted green or black with white trim, and sometimes tall white roof spires.

clues.title: Road: straight dam with water on one side
text: The **Afsluitdijk** is a very recognizable man-made causeway between Noord-Holland and Friesland. It is a divided highway that runs in a very straight southwest to northeast direction. You can see water to your southeast, and a dike to your northwest.
NOTE: There are other large causeways and dams in the Netherlands, but the Afsluitdijk is the biggest and has a very recognizable road direction.
clues.summary: A long straight divided highway on a dam running southwest to northeast, with water to the southeast and a dike to the northwest. Other big dams exist but this is the biggest.

clues.title: Landscape: greenhouses everywhere
text: In the Westland municipality, just southwest of The Hague, **greenhouses** are extremely common. They cover most of the municipality’s land surface.
clues.summary: Greenhouses cover most of the land in one municipality southwest of The Hague.

clues.title: Coverage: trekker with brown hair visible
text: In the southern part of the Veluwe, in** National Park De Hoge Veluwe**, you can find a trekker that is recognizable because the Google employee’s brown hair is visible.
clues.summary: In a national park in the central forest area, a trekker shows the brown hair of the Google employee.

clues.title: Landmark: huge harbour with round fuel tanks
text: The **harbour of Rotterdam** is one of the largest in the world. It extends all the way from downtown Rotterdam to the North Sea coast. If you see a lot of industrial activity, often in combination with large, round **fuel storage tanks**, there is a good chance that you are in this harbour area.
NOTE: Amsterdam and Delfzijl also have large harbours. Both also feature a lot of [fuel storage tanks](https://goo.gl/maps/c6f3u3iLbD5yGCk47).
clues.summary: The Rotterdam harbour runs from downtown to the coast. Heavy industry and large round fuel tanks suggest it. Amsterdam and Delfzijl harbours also have fuel tanks.

clues.title: Street sign: neighbourhood name plus number
text: Many **streets in Lelystad** follow a fairly distinct naming scheme: instead of having unique names, they are named after the neighbourhood they are in, followed by a number. Some of these neighbourhood names show up on the Google map.
clues.summary: Many streets in Lelystad are named after their neighbourhood followed by a number. Some of these names show on the map.

clues.title: Border: Belgian enclaves in town
text: **Baarle** is a town in the south of the Netherlands which contains a number of Belgian enclaves. Throughout the town, you can sometimes see signs of this, such as markings on the pavement and [Dutch and Belgian flags](https://goo.gl/maps/sKCBPk8vqM9AUrmB9) being flown together.
clues.summary: A southern town contains Belgian enclaves, shown by pavement markings and Dutch and Belgian flags flown together.

clues.title: Sign: pedestrian figure with starfish limbs
text: Netherlands' guy has **funny limbs**, they shrink towards the end sorta like a starfish.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: The figure has funny limbs that shrink toward the end, like a starfish.

clues.title: Houses: many tall skyscrapers
text: If you know your in The Netherlands, and you see many tall buildings, you will most likely be in Rotterdam. This city has the majority of skyscrapers within The Netherlands.
NOTE: The Hague and Amsterdam also have some tall buildings but not as much as Rotterdam.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: If you know you are in the country and see many tall buildings, it is most likely Rotterdam, which has most of the skyscrapers. The Hague and Amsterdam have some too.
